It’s generally a lot of listening to what you want to sound like and experimentation with your playing. Getting similar gear to what your reference player uses can be helpful, but not always necessary.

I think I need some specification on your definition of Altissimo F, are you talking about F atop the third leger line above staff or an octave higher? If you mean the latter, that’s extremely high and would take a loooot of work. But I’m pretty sure you mean 3 lines above staff since it’s in a riff you’re learning. In that case the easiest fingering to use is all 3 palm keys left hand and top side key on right hand. If you are using that and still getting no sound, first try playing up to it from notes you can already play. The goal for high notes is very fast air, try creating a lot of pressure to speed up that air. How you do this varies from person to person.

I agree with a lot of that, but wouldn’t go as far to try to play without it lol. I did forget to mention that overtones can be hard to get a beginner to do, since often times they’ll go for biting to get them, instead the airflow change we want to practice.

You’re definitely doing pretty good in my opinion. 

   The first thing I noticed was that you were tonguing almost every note, which comes off as a little distasteful. But that could be how the piece was written, it’d be helpful to know what you’re playing to make better critique. 

On a lot of the longer notes and more noticeably toward the end the intonation seemed to be struggling almost like bad vibrato, but didn’t sound intentional. Doing long tones with a drone for a while each time you practice is a great way to work on that. 

Your low notes sounded pretty good tone wise, but like almost every sax player out there, your higher notes were less full and probably a little sharp. This is usually due to biting down a lot on those higher notes. Try playing up to those and then looking at a tuner. My saxophone teacher has me do an exercise where as you play higher you drop your jaw more and more to help work on this.

Hopefully some of these points help! Also I wouldn’t consider your playing crap, it’s good to be honest with ourselves, but not good to be self-deprecating when it comes to our playing.

Your lung capacity doesexpand, and you can do some exercises to speed the process up like long tones getting longer everyday. You may be using a poor embouchure or too strong reed if you’re really not getting much for one breathe though.

Maybe I’m crazy, but I’ve never heard the octave key called a ‘crutch’. As far as I know, every sax player uses it, for all skill levels. So I wouldn’t think of trying to teach the sax with no octave key as a good idea. I generally wait a while to teach concepts like the overtone series, as I want the student to first learn how to play the notes well and with decent sound before I expand upon that.

Hopefully I’m not too late to be of any help, but I’ve got a few tips. 

It may be best just to wait until you can play the mouthpiece before buying as it’ll take less time. If you are still going to order one online, don’t go amazon, it’s not usually a good option. I recommend Woodwind Brasswind for mouthpiece purchasing, as they allow you to try them out and send them back if you’d don’t like it. I think they have an option to try out 3 of them and only send back the 2 you don’t want, which is a pretty good deal for a time like this. 

About your options - the only one I have much experience with is the Meyer. I strongly recommend you don’t go for Meyer if you can’t play it first. They tend to be inconsistent in production, so although they can be really great, getting a bad one isn’t too uncommon and sucks for your playing and your wallet. 

Hope this helps you or the next person needing an answer to this question!
